query: Earlier empirical-potential and first-principles studies primarily targeted phase-transition temperature, while other fusion properties remain difficult because they require free energies on both sides of the transition with vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling retained. Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation is highly accurate but depends on costly molecular dynamics. TOR-TILD increased throughput for elemental and binary systems, yet slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems. Under the constraint that the free energies of both solid and fluid states and the relevant entropy terms remain faithful, what single testable methodological hypothesis could substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties? State the proposed intervention and why it should work, predict its speed and fidelity relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD, define composition and temperature boundaries, cite supporting evidence from prior elemental or binary results, and specify a decisive benchmark of phase free energies and derived observables that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A machine-learning based surrogate model, trained on a limited set of explicit ab initio molecular dynamics data for both solid and fluid phases, can accurately predict the full free-energy landscape—including vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling—thus substantially reducing computational cost in determining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties of multicomponent high-entropy systems.
generation.material_initial_state: Multicomponent high-entropy alloys (and analogous fusion materials) in their solid and fluid states, modeled at high temperatures near their fusion regimes.
generation.intervention: Develop and implement an ML surrogate (for example, using moment tensor potentials or a comparable interatomic machine learning framework) trained on a sparse dataset extracted from high-fidelity ab initio MD calculations. The training set will target key points along both solid and fluid free-energy curves ensuring retention of relevant entropy contributions.
generation.conditions: The surrogate will be applied over a temperature range approaching fusion (e.g., from ~0.9 T_m up to fusion temperatures) under conditions where vibrational entropy, anharmonic effects, and electron–vibration contributions are critical. These simulations should mimic conditions of both near-melting solid and fully developed fluid states.
generation.structural_mediator: The local atomic configurations and bonding environments captured by the ML potential, which map the complex interatomic interactions that govern the free energy in both phases.
generation.mechanism: By learning the high-dimensional free-energy landscape from a representative and computationally affordable subset of ab initio MD data, the surrogate model interpolates the thermodynamic properties with high fidelity. This reduces the need for extensive and computationally expensive simulations (as in TOR-TILD) while preserving the critical entropy and anharmonic contributions.
generation.predicted_outcome: The ML surrogate is expected to achieve an order-of-magnitude speedup relative to explicit ab initio MD/TOR-TILD methods while maintaining prediction accuracies within approximately 5% error for fusion free energies and related observables.
generation.baseline: Conventional explicit ab initio MD free-energy computations and the TOR-TILD approach, which provide high accuracy but at a prohibitive cost for multicomponent systems.
generation.boundary: This method is anticipated to be valid for multicomponent (up to ~5-element) high-entropy systems in the temperature regimes relevant to fusion and high-temperature thermodynamics. Its performance beyond these composition and temperature limits remains to be ascertained.
generation.uncertainty: It remains uncertain how well the surrogate will capture extreme anharmonic effects and subtle electron–vibration coupling at the highest temperatures; additional calibration and validation may be needed under these conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a representative multicomponent high-entropy alloy system and perform a series of explicit ab initio MD/TOR-TILD simulations to determine its fusion free energy and associated entropy contributions across both solid and fluid states. Next, train the ML surrogate model on a limited dataset taken from these simulations. Use the trained model to predict free energies and derived observables at conditions not included in the training set. Compare these predictions with the high-fidelity simulation results.
measurements: Indicators of anharmonicity and electron–vibration coupling
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ML surrogate’s predicted free energies differ by more than 5% from those obtained via explicit ab initio MD/TOR-TILD simulations, or if the computational speedup is not at least an order-of-magnitude faster, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

Instead, we would like to use the results obtained thus far for MoNbTiTa to analyze the strengthening and ductility behavior in a broader range of refractory alloys. One way to achieve this would be to define a set of “good” descriptors and train a black box ML model, which can then be used to obtain properties at arbitrary compositions. Such descriptors may encompass purely local structural characteristics, effective interatomic interactions or local electronic structure-related properties like moments of the local density of states and energies of simpler substructures,. In this section, we discuss the results of the development of the interatomic-potential model used to enable the application of MD simulations of dislocation properties in bcc MoNbTaW. We employ the general framework of machine-learning (ML)-based approaches, which have emerged recently as a systematic framework to develop potentials with accuracies near that of the underlying DFT calculations for elemental and multicomponent systems,. Here, using training data reported previously for elemental, binary, ternary, and quaternary systems in Nb–Ta–Mo–W, we developed a potential for the MoNbTaW RHEA based on the moment tensor potential (MTP) formalism, which has been found to feature an excellent balance between accuracy and computational cost. The basic materials property predictions of the MTP model are provided in Supplementary Table 1.
